title: Support herdr protocol 20 (server auto-updated to 0.8.2 mid-run)
description:
The herdr server on this machine auto-updated from 0.8.0 (protocol 19) to 0.8.2 (protocol 20) DURING an epic run. internal/herd/client/protocol.go pins ProtocolVersion = 19, so every tk herd command immediately failed:

  Error: connecting to herdr: herd/client: herdr protocol mismatch at ~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock: server reports protocol 20 (herdr 0.8.2), this client is pinned to protocol 19 — refusing to continue

The refusal itself is correct and well-worded. The problem is that a background server upgrade hard-stops every in-flight run with no path forward, and the operator cannot downgrade or restart the server without killing OTHER runs sharing it (there were six workers from another repo live at the time).

Bumping the constant alone is NOT the fix: it turns internal/herd/{cleanup,client,...} red because the client tests replay CAPTURED protocol-19 responses (fakeserver_test.go, metadata_test.go, and comments through events.go and protocol.go all pin 0.8.0/19). Re-verify the wire shapes against 0.8.2 and re-capture, rather than editing the number and hoping.

Work:
1. Diff protocol 19 vs 20 (herdr api schema --json against the running server) and record what actually changed.
2. Re-capture the fixtures and update the version comments.
3. Decide the compatibility policy: an exact pin means any server upgrade is a hard stop for every user, which is severe for a tool the operator does not control the update cadence of. Consider a supported RANGE with a documented minimum, so a forward-compatible server upgrade degrades to a warning rather than a refusal — while keeping the hard stop for a genuinely incompatible protocol.

Workaround used to finish the current run: a locally built tk with the constant bumped, NOT committed. Read-only calls and worktree.remove were verified working against protocol 20 before relying on it.
acceptance_criteria: tk herd works against herdr 0.8.2/protocol 20 with the internal/herd suite green; the fixtures are re-captured from the running server rather than hand-edited; the compatibility policy (exact pin vs supported range) is decided and documented, and a server newer than the pin fails or warns according to that policy.
